exam: What bedside sign would you use first to assess perfusion in an infant? — Capillary refill time >3s indicates poor perfusion.
You suspect malaria‑related shock; what is the next best test? — Rapid malaria test; if positive, start antimalarial immediately.
A child with shock has a normal blood pressure but weak pulses; what is the most likely type of shock? — Distributive (septic) shock.
You have a child with shock and oliguria; what is the first investigation? — Urine output monitoring and serum electrolytes.
If a child in shock has a glucose of 2.0 mmol/L, what should you do? — Give 10% dextrose IV and repeat glucose in 15 min.
You are in a setting without a BP cuff; how do you estimate blood pressure? — Use the pulse pressure and capillary refill as proxies.
A child with shock is not improving after fluids; what is the next step? — Start dopamine infusion and consider cardiac ultrasound if available.
ai.title: Shock in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Shock is a life‑threatening state of inadequate tissue perfusion. Recognise it early, identify the underlying cause, and start resuscitation while awaiting definitive treatment.

sections.p: Shock is defined by a sustained drop in organ perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia. In children, the classic triad is tachycardia, weak pulses, and cool extremities, but signs vary with age.
The Pediatric Early Warning Score (PEWS) helps stage shock severity. A score >5 warrants urgent review and possible escalation to intensive care.

t.b: Heart rate, respiratory rate, cap refill, level of consciousness, perfusion

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Follow the hierarchy: infectious, cardiac, endocrine, hypovolaemic, obstructive, distributive.

b: Infants: poor feeding, irritability, sunken fontanelle
Children: tachypnoea, pallor, delayed cap refill
Older children: confusion, hypotension, cold extremities
sections.p: Presentation depends on age and cause. Common features: tachycardia, weak pulses, altered consciousness, pallor, cyanosis, and in infants, poor feeding and lethargy.
Prioritise bedside tests; send samples if available. Use the table for each test’s purpose and interpretation.

t.b: Low Hb suggests anaemia; high WCC suggests infection
Hyponatraemia or hyperkalaemia can worsen shock

sections.p: Look for signs of organ failure: oliguria, altered mental status, metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, and bleeding.

b: Start broad‑spectrum antibiotics if sepsis suspected
Give oral rehydration or IV fluids (20–30 ml/kg)
Use vasopressors (dopamine) only if fluids fail
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Use simple, evidence‑based protocols suitable for low‑resource settings.

b: Educate on hand hygiene and vaccination
sections.p: Monitor vital signs every 15–30 min until stable. Prevent recurrence by treating infections early, ensuring immunisations, and educating caregivers.
